nameStory: The name 'speedwell' comes from an old English farewell blessing meaning 'may you prosper' or 'godspeed,' given to travelers for good luck on their journeys. Early herbalists believed these little blue flowers had protective powers and would keep you safe on the road. The 'broadleaf' part simply refers to this species having wider leaves than most of its speedwell cousins.
description: Broadleaf speedwell is a low-growing perennial herb that forms spreading mats or clumps in gardens and disturbed areas. It reaches about 6-12 inches tall with sturdy, somewhat hairy stems that can sprawl along the ground before turning upward. The plant produces clusters of small, bright blue flowers with white centers that bloom from late spring through summer. This European native has naturalized in parts of New England, though it's not as common as some of its speedwell relatives.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small bright blue flowers with four petals and white centers, arranged in dense, spike-like clusters at the stem tips. Each flower is only about 1/4 inch across but they're grouped together in showy displays that catch your eye from a distance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to lance-shaped leaves that are noticeably broader than other speedwells, with toothed edges that feel slightly rough to the touch. Leaves are arranged in opposite pairs along the stem and have a somewhat wrinkled, textured surface.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading patches with stems that creep along the ground before turning upward to bloom. The whole plant has a somewhat fuzzy appearance due to fine hairs covering the stems and leaves.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Produces small, heart-shaped seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny brown seeds. The capsules are flattened and notched at the top, creating the distinctive heart shape.

habitat: Broadleaf speedwell prefers sunny to partially shaded spots in gardens, roadsides, and disturbed soils throughout New England. It thrives in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and is often found in cultivated areas, along paths, and in grassy openings. This species is more commonly encountered in southern New England than in the northern regions.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges early with fresh green leaves forming low mats. Flower buds begin developing in late spring as stems start to elongate upward.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright blue flower spikes most prominent from June through August. Seeds develop and ripen in late summer capsules.
seasonality.fall: Flowering may continue into early fall in favorable conditions. Leaves remain green well into autumn before dying back.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level, surviving as underground roots and crown. Look for dried brown stems and old seed capsules in protected spots.

funFact: Despite being called 'speedwell' for bringing good luck to travelers, this plant is actually quite the homebody - it spreads primarily by creeping underground stems rather than relying on seeds to disperse to new locations, preferring to slowly expand its territory rather than venture far from home.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other blue-flowered speedwells, especially Germander speedwell, but broadleaf speedwell has noticeably wider, more oval leaves and denser flower clusters. Remember: 'broadleaf' means broader leaves than its speedwell siblings, and the flowers form thick, crowded spikes rather than loose, airy clusters.
contextualKnowledge: Broadleaf speedwell is sometimes called 'Hungarian speedwell' in older references, reflecting its European origins. Gardeners may know it as an ornamental ground cover that can become weedy, and it's often found escaping from cultivation rather than growing truly wild.
compareHints: Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements. Germander speedwell has similar blue flowers but grows more upright with heart-shaped leaves, while the tiny thyme-leaved speedwell has thread-like leaves and scattered individual flowers rather than showy clusters.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
